title: At the café
goal: Order food and drinks, pay, and use *poproszę* — the most useful word a visitor to Poland can have.
bekal: answer the waiter's questions about seating and how you'll pay
ask for something politely with *czy mogę prosić o…*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — W kawiarni
dialogs.intro: A small café next to campus, four in the afternoon. The waiter comes over with a notepad.

lines.speaker: Kelner:
lines.id: Good afternoon. What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'll have a large coffee and a sernik, please.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Dla mnie herbatę z cytryną, proszę.
lines.id: Tea with lemon for me, please.
lines.literal: for me tea with lemon, please.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Na miejscu. Czy jest wolny stolik przy oknie?
lines.id: For here. Is there a free table by the window?
lines.literal: on place. whether is free table by window?

lines.speaker: Kelner:
lines.id: Of course. Paying by card or cash?

lines.speaker: Kelner:
lines.id: Fine. I'll bring it right away.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Przepraszam, czy mogę prosić o wodę?
lines.id: Excuse me, could I have some water?
lines.literal: sorry, whether I-may ask about water?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Still, thanks. And the bill, please.

notes: **Poproszę** is the magic word in Poland. Literally "I will ask for", it's used just like "I'll have" or "please" — and it's considered more polite than *chcę* (I want), which sounds demanding. It's always followed by the **object** form: *poproszę kawę*, *poproszę rachunek*.
**Dużą kawę** — both words change. The adjective *duża* becomes *dużą*, the noun *kawa* becomes *kawę*. This is the Unit 7 rule in real use; if this part feels heavy, go back there for a moment.
**Dla mnie** means "for me" and is used constantly when ordering together. Its twins: *dla niego* (for him), *dla niej* (for her), *dla nas* (for us).
**A dla pani?** Waiters address you with *pan* / *pani*, never *ty*. You should reply with *pan* / *pani* too if you want to ask back: *A pan co poleca?* (What would you recommend?)

**Kartą, gotówką** — the ending *-ą* again, but this time not an object but an **instrument**. The *narzędnik* form you know from *jestem studentem* is also used to say "with what" or "by what": *piszę długopisem* (I write with a pen), *jadę autobusem* (I go by bus).
**Na miejscu czy na wynos** is a question you're sure to hear in every Polish café. Learn the answers now so you won't freeze: *na miejscu* (for here) or *na wynos* (to go).
**Czy mogę prosić o…** is the most polite request formula, usable anywhere — restaurant, office, street. After *o* always comes the object form: *o wodę*, *o rachunek*, *o pomoc*.

**Sernik** (cheesecake) is one of three cakes found in almost every Polish café, along with *szarlotka* (apple pie) and *makowiec* (poppy seed cake). Ordering one without hesitation makes you sound like someone who knows the place.

grammars.title: Ordering: poproszę + object
body: One formula that covers almost every buying-and-selling situation in Poland.
after: The last row is the most refined form, and it differs by the gender of the **speaker**: a man says *chciałbym*, a woman *chciałabym*. It's a conditional form that really belongs to A2 — just use it as a memorized chunk.

⚠️ Avoid *chcę kawę* when ordering. It's grammatically correct, but it sounds like "I want coffee, now". The difference in politeness is about the gap between "gimme a coffee" and "could I have a coffee".

grammars.title: Narzędnik — with what, by what
body: The same ending as after *jestem*, used for tools, vehicles, and companions.
after: The endings are exactly as in Unit 2: **-em** for masculine and neuter words, **-ą** for feminine words.

Look at the "together with whom" row: *z* here means "with". The same word also means "from" (*jestem z Indonezji*), and what tells them apart is the noun's ending — more proof that in Polish the ending does the work, not the preposition.

blocks.text: The last three names are the dishes tourists ask about most. *Bigos* and *żurek* have almost no equivalent in any cuisine you know — order them once to find out, then decide for yourself.

blocks.title: If you have dietary restrictions
items: *Nie jem mięsa.* — I don't eat meat.
*Nie jem wieprzowiny.* — I don't eat pork.
*Czy to jest bez mięsa?* — Is this meat-free?
*Czy w tym jest wieprzowina?* — Is there pork in this?

blocks.title: Three things to know before you walk in
items: **Water isn't free.** In Polish restaurants water is always ordered and paid for, and the waiter will ask *gazowana czy niegazowana*.
**A tip of about ten percent** is usual in restaurants, but not expected in small cafés. Saying *reszty nie trzeba* is enough — don't just leave money on the table without a word.
**Smacznego** is said by the waiter when bringing food, and also by strangers at the next table. Reply with *dziękuję*.

exercises.prompt: Order each item with *poproszę*. Watch the ending.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Poproszę kawę. — Poproszę herbatę. — Poproszę sernik. — Poproszę wodę. — Poproszę zupę. — Poproszę piwo.
Poproszę dużą kawę. — Na miejscu, nie na wynos. — Czy mogę prosić o wodę? — Rachunek, proszę. — Nie jem mięsa.
Poproszę dużą kawę. — Na miejscu czy na wynos? — Rachunek, proszę. — Czy mogę prosić o wodę? — Płacę kartą.
wave: Read the Unit 6 dialogue out loud, then order five different items with *poproszę* — without looking at the ending table.
